description: a qkd network qkdn consists of interconnected nodes linked via optical fiber or free space channels to execute qkd protocols. qkdns are considered a key step towards the realization of the quantum internet a future global network of quantum information processors designed to interconnect next generation quantum computers. conceived as a complement to the classical internet the quantum internet will enable end to end qkd and support novel network functionalities beyond those of today’s communication systems . to take full advantage of the benefits offered by qkd protocols while ensuring efficient key management storage and integration with classical infrastructure it is essential to design a layered architecture tailored to this emerging technology see <Reference> . various approaches have been proposed as the design of qkd network architectures remains an open topic and a dedicated etsi report is expected by the end of 2025 . nonetheless there is broad consensus on including qkdn management and control layers between the user or application layer and the physical infrastructure. these two intermediate layers coordinate the dynamic operation and overall supervision of the network by handling session control key relay routing link configuration performance monitoring and enforcement of security and quality policies .

<Reference> supports our main premise: a single execution of the protocol must yield at least secret key bits as specified by the user so that re execution is not needed. however in deriving eqs. and we imposed a second requirement: the qber must be estimated with sufficient accuracy see eq. . we observed that this constraint becomes more restrictive at shorter link distances even though we defined to reduce its impact. in such scenarios the number of secret bits generated often exceeds by a large margin. this raises a relevant question: is our strategy still efficient under these conditions? could we for instance introduce controlled amounts of additional noise to slightly increase the qber making it easier to estimate accurately while potentially requiring fewer initial photons? this is an interesting point since introducing artificial noise would indeed lower the number of photons needed at the shortest distances while photon losses would remain unchanged. the trade offs would be a smaller value of since cascade requires more parity checks to correct more errors and therefore exposes more key information and the need for additional processing to recover the true qber of the quantum channel from the artificially altered raw keys. preliminary tests show that this approach can substantially reduce at the smallest link distances. however a more thorough analysis is necessary to confirm and complete these results. this would overly extend the scope of this thesis and is left for future research. the answer would be affirmative if after execution only bits were delivered to the user and the remaining bits were discarded. however this is not the case as the key manager stores any excess key material for future use. in this context artificially increasing the qber would lower the key bit rate kbr ultimately making the protocol less efficient. therefore preserving the original noise level remains the more practical and resource conscious approach.

qwerty based visualization of how the example quantum phase estimation program in <Reference> constructs the desired fourier basis state quantum computers have leaped from the theoretical realm into a race to large scale implementations. this is due to the promise of revolutionary speedups where achieving such speedup requires designing an algorithm that harnesses the structure of a problem using quantum mechanics. yet many quantum programming languages today require programmers to reason at a low level of physics notation and quantum gate circuitry. this presents a significant barrier to entry for programmers who have not yet built up an intuition about quantum gate semantics and it can prove to be tedious even for those who have. in this paper we present qwerty a new quantum programming language that allows programmers to manipulate qubits more expressively than gates and trace programs without bra ket notation. due to its novel basis type and easy interoperability with python qwerty is a powerful framework for high level quantum classical computation.

one can interpret a superposition of computational basis vectors as a signal in the time domain whereas period finding warrants analysis in the frequency domain which period finding achieves by measuring in the fourier basis. line of <Reference> step of <Reference> the final quantum step of period finding can be understood by imagining the state beforehand a superposition of inputs that produce the same output as a signal in the time domain. in the same sense that a time signal is a weighted sum of functions with different frequencies a discrete fourier series the superposition of inputs to that produce the same output is itself a weighted superposition of fourier basis states. measurement in the fourier basis thus reveals which fourier basis states frequencies are in this superposition. because each of these frequencies measured are multiples of the fundamental frequency the fundamental frequency can be extracted classically from sampled measurements. the reciprocal of this fundamental frequency is the desired fundamental period: for example the fundamental period of the example function defined on line of <Reference>.
